The caption explicitly states a fetal double-bubble sign with polyhydramnios, which is the classic prenatal sonographic manifestation of duodenal atresia; the image shows the corresponding dilated fluid-filled stomach and proximal duodenum. Real patient image, no third-party copyright, no diagram/chart, and the finding is directly attributable to duodenal atresia. Polyhydramnios is captioned but absent from the vocabulary, so it is listed as a proposed finding.

in_text_mentions: tion demonstrated duodenal obstruction with situs anomaly, and intraoperative assessment revealed non-rotation without pathological fixation or a narrow mesenteric pedicle. Because the mesentery was already broadly based, no Ladd procedure or additional mesenteric widening was required. Laparoscopic duodenoduodenostomy was therefore performed without major technical modification (Figure 3). These case-specific findings suggest that the operative complexity in patients with situs anomaly is influenced primarily by the associated rotational anatomy rather than by the duodenal anastomosis itself.

panels.rationale: Single-panel fetal ultrasound from a case report titled 'Hemorrhage from Umbilical Cord Ulceration Identified on Real-Time Ultrasound in a Fetus with Duodenal Atresia.' The image shows real-time fetal blood swirling (arrows) from the umbilical cord into amniotic fluid, adjacent to a transverse view of the fetal abdomen/pelvis. The in-text confirms the same ultrasound demonstrated the double-bubble sign and polyhydramnios, diagnostic of duodenal atresia. The umbilical cord ulceration/hemorrhage is a recognized complication of duodenal atresia in this disease-focused article. The double-bubble sign is supported by the in-text and the captioned transverse abdominal view; the umbilical cord hemorrhage is clearly visible (arrows) but absent from the vocabulary, so it is placed in proposed_findings. Typicality is variant because the panel highlights the less-common umbilical cord ulceration complication rather than the textbook double-bubble alone. Age group is child (fetus/newborn infant delivered per in-text). No skin, ethnicity, or stage applicable.

An ultrasound confirmed the double bubble sign and polyhydramnios. Blood was observed in real-time swirling into the amniotic fluid from the umbilical cord (Figure 1). The patient was taken to the operating room and an emergent cesarean section was performed. The amniotic fluid was grossly bloody. A viable male infant weighing 2295 grams was delivered with Apgar scores of 7 and 8 at one and five minutes, respectively.

panels.rationale: Single frontal infant chest/abdominal radiograph (CXR/KUB) from a case report whose article title and caption identify duodenal atresia. The image shows the textbook double-bubble sign (two gas-filled upper-abdominal bubbles with a relatively gasless distal abdomen), a real human-patient radiographic manifestation of duodenal atresia, corroborated by the in-text mention that plain films showed the double-bubble sign. The elevated left hemidiaphragm and transposed umbilical lines are concurrent findings but are not disease-attribution evidence; the panel is included for the duodenal atresia double-bubble sign only. No stated ethnicity, no assessable skin, and no annotations are present.

in_text_mentions: Abdominal plain films showed double‐bubble sign concerning for duodenal atresia, which was confirmed on ultrasound day of life 1 (Fig. 4). The patient underwent uncomplicated surgical repair of the atresia on day of life 5. Patient continued to have poor feeding and severe reflux with esophageal and gastric dysmotility. He underwent a fundoplication and percutaneous gastrostomy tube placement at 2 months of age.

From birth, patient was noted on serial imaging to have an elevated left hemidiaphragm (Fig. 4). He underwent dynamic studies which demonstrated relative akinesia compared to the right hemidiaphragm consistent with left hemidiaphragm eventration. He underwent plication day of life 27, which required patching at two months of life due to failed plication. Patient continued to have respiratory insufficiency progressing to respiratory failure and required tracheostomy placement at 9 months.
